new_statements.second_reader_evidence: PDF metadata 'Gwara wordlist paper 09.doc', created 20 May 2009; 27 pp.; text layer present, no scanned needed). Section 3.3 'Tones' on p. 4 (extracted text page 6 of the file) reads exactly: 'Gwara has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. The basic conventions are as follows; [High/Mid Unmarked/Low/Rising/Falling table] All syllables are marked for tone in the present document. Thus any unmarked syllables should be assumed to be mid. A number of words exhibit three tone heights in one word, illustrating the contrast. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only prosodic description is tonal: three level tones (high, mid, low) plus rising and falling glides on every syllable, with tone also marking noun plurals. Stress is not mentioned at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author notes the transcription is preliminary (one elicitation session, 20 April 2009) and the draft is marked 'not for citation without reference to the author'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on citation forms from a wordlist; no phrase-level or sentence prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Gwara (autonym iGwara; Hausa 'Gora') of villages Gora A-E, Jaba and Kagarko LGAs, Kaduna State, Nigeria; Koro cluster, NW Plateau, closest to Idũ/Dũya (idun1241). Blench states it is NOT the 'Idon-Gora-Ankwe' of Crozier & Blench 1992. Matches gwar1240 exactly; no ISO code. Under 3,000 speakers, threatened.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2009. Gwara, an unknown language of Central Nigeria: Phonology, wordlist and suggestions for orthography. Draft circulated for comment (printout 20 May 2009), 27 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation.
sources.quote: Gwara has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. [...] All syllables are marked for tone in the present document. Thus any unmarked syllables should be assumed to be mid. A number of words exhibit three tone heights in one word, illustrating the contrast. [...] Falling tone is very important and is often a significant marker of plurals in nouns.
sources.note: Nothing about stress. Section 3 Phonology (pp. 2-5) covers vowels, consonants and 3.3 Tones: three level tones (H, M, L) plus rising and falling glides, every syllable tone-marked; tonal plurals. The words stress/accent/prominence/intonation/pitch do not occur anywhere in the 27-page text layer. Data are from one elicitation session (20 Apr 2009, Gora A); transcription called preliminary.
